title: Attention Is All You Need
hook: A new architecture for relating words across a sequence.
idea: The Transformer uses attention to let each word draw on relevant parts of the input. Instead of processing a sentence strictly one step at a time, much of its training can be parallelized.
analogy: Imagine a translator highlighting every other word that helps interpret the word currently being translated. Different attention heads can learn different relationships.
why: The architecture became a foundation for many later language models. This paper studied translation; it did not introduce ChatGPT or prove that attention alone produces general intelligence.
read: Start with the abstract and introduction. In Section 3, look at Figure 1 and the descriptions of attention and multi-head attention. Then inspect the translation results and conclusion.
question: What changes when each word can use information from other words directly?
terms: A learned way to weight which parts of a sequence matter for a particular representation.
A neural-network architecture built around attention and feed-forward layers.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
hook: Learn general language representations before specializing.
idea: BERT first learns from large amounts of unlabeled text using tasks such as predicting masked words. It can then be fine-tuned for a variety of language-understanding tasks.
analogy: A reader learns general language by filling gaps in sentences, then takes a short course for a particular job.
why: It showed the value of reusable contextual language representations. BERT reads context in both directions; it is not the same kind of next-token generator as GPT.
read: Read the abstract and introduction, then Section 3 and Figure 1. Skim the task results and consider the cost of pre-training versus downstream fine-tuning.
question: Why might a general language education help with many separate tasks?
terms: A broad initial learning stage, typically using large datasets.
Further training that adapts a pre-trained model to a task.

title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
hook: Measure how language-model loss changes with resources.
idea: The authors observed regular relationships between prediction loss and model size, dataset size, and training compute across their experiments.
analogy: Like plotting fuel use against engine size, a trend can guide planning without guaranteeing the performance of every future design.
why: Scaling studies made resource allocation a measurable research question. These empirical laws depend on the training setup and do not predict all real-world capabilities or guarantee truthfulness.
read: Read the abstract and introduction, then examine the main plots and conclusions. Focus on what the axes measure rather than trying to derive each equation.
question: What exactly is being predicted, and under what experimental conditions?
terms: A numeric measure of prediction error used during training.
The computational work used to train or run a model.

title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
hook: Use examples in a prompt to specify a new task.
idea: GPT-3 was evaluated on tasks described through text and a few examples in the prompt, without changing model weights for each task.
analogy: Give a well-read assistant a few examples of how to format an answer, and ask it to continue the pattern.
why: The paper helped establish prompting as a flexible interface. It also documents tasks where performance struggled and issues such as training-data contamination.
read: Read the abstract, introduction and Figure 1; compare zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot setups. Review limitations before drawing conclusions from benchmark scores.
question: What is learned during training, and what is merely supplied in the prompt?
terms: Providing a small number of examples in the prompt.
A learned numerical value inside a model.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
hook: Consult external documents while generating an answer.
idea: RAG combines a retriever that finds relevant passages with a generator that uses those passages. The paper studies a trainable combination using a Wikipedia index.
analogy: An open-book exam: look up a relevant page before composing an answer.
why: It provides a way to access external knowledge. Retrieval errors and unsupported generation still occur; external documents do not automatically make an answer true.
read: Read the introduction, architecture figure and retrieval formulations, then compare question-answering results.
question: What happens if the retrieved documents are wrong or irrelevant?
terms: A system that finds passages relevant to a query.
Connecting an answer to supporting evidence.

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
hook: Adapt a model by training a much smaller set of weights.
idea: LoRA freezes the original model weights and trains small low-rank matrices that represent updates to selected weights.
analogy: Instead of rewriting an entire reference book for a new role, add a compact set of specialized annotations.
why: It can reduce the number of trainable parameters and memory needed for adaptation. Savings depend on the model and setup; it does not eliminate the cost of the original model.
read: Read the abstract and introduction; use the architecture figure to see where the small matrices sit. Then compare the experiment tables and limitations.
question: Which weights are frozen, and which are actually trained?
terms: A compact mathematical representation using smaller matrices.
A small trainable addition used to specialize a larger model.

title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
hook: Use selected parts of a large network for each token.
idea: A router directs each token to one feed-forward expert in a sparse model, increasing total capacity without using all experts for every token.
analogy: A specialist department sends each case to one expert rather than asking every employee to handle it.
why: Sparse activation can improve capacity per unit of computation, but storing and communicating between experts remains costly.
read: Start with the routing diagram, then read the sections on stability and load balancing before the speed comparisons.
question: Why are total parameters different from active parameters?
terms: A subnetwork selected to process particular inputs.
A learned component that chooses which expert receives an input.

title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
hook: Train models to better follow what people ask.
idea: The authors combine demonstrations, human rankings of outputs, and reinforcement learning to produce InstructGPT models that better follow instructions in their evaluation.
analogy: A trainee first studies worked examples, then receives preferences comparing several possible answers.
why: The work illustrates why capability and following human preferences are different goals. Human preferences are imperfect and the resulting model can still make mistakes.
read: Read the abstract and introduction, then Figure 2 for the training stages. Look at evaluation methods, results and limitations.
question: What behavior is rewarded, and whose judgments define a better answer?
terms: Reinforcement learning from human feedback; feedback is used to guide model behavior.
The broad problem of making AI behavior accord with intended goals and values.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
hook: Reduce expensive data movement during attention.
idea: FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention computation into blocks, reducing transfers between slower high-bandwidth GPU memory and faster on-chip memory.
analogy: A chef works on ingredients in manageable batches on the countertop instead of repeatedly walking back to the storeroom.
why: The paper demonstrates that moving data can be as important as the number of arithmetic operations. Its speedups depend on hardware, sequence length and the baseline.
read: Read the abstract and introduction, then Figure 1 and the explanation of memory hierarchy. Review the experimental setup before interpreting speedup numbers.
question: Why can doing the same calculation with fewer memory transfers be faster?
terms: Different memory locations have different capacities and access speeds.
Computes the standard attention operation rather than an approximation, subject to numerical precision.

title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
hook: Show worked examples with intermediate steps.
idea: The paper supplies examples that include intermediate reasoning steps in the prompt. It finds improvements on several reasoning tasks for sufficiently large models.
analogy: A math workbook shows the working as well as the answer, giving the learner a pattern to follow.
why: Prompt design can change task performance without training new weights. Extra steps cost tokens and can contain mistakes.
read: Read the example prompts first, compare standard and chain-of-thought prompting, then inspect task results and limitations.
question: Can a plausible explanation still lead to an incorrect answer?
terms: The input text supplied to a language model.
A demonstration included in the prompt.

title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
hook: Balance model size and training data within a budget.
idea: The authors study how to divide a fixed training-compute budget between the number of parameters and training tokens, then test their allocation with Chinchilla.
analogy: A bigger factory is not useful if it receives too little raw material; capacity and supply need to grow together.
why: It challenged training practices that emphasized parameter count. A compute-optimal training recipe does not necessarily minimize lifetime serving costs.
read: Read the introduction and scaling plots, then compare Chinchilla with Gopher under the stated training budget.
question: Optimal for training cost, inference cost, or another objective?
terms: A chunk of text processed by a model.
The total computational work available for an experiment.

title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
hook: Interleave planning with actions and observations.
idea: ReAct prompts a model to alternate intermediate reasoning with actions, such as querying an external source, and to use observations in its next steps.
analogy: An analyst writes a plan, looks up evidence, and adjusts the plan after seeing the result.
why: It connects language models to interactive tasks and tools. Tool errors and accumulated mistakes can still derail a sequence.
read: Begin with the trajectory examples and method overview, then compare the question-answering and interactive-task experiments.
question: Which action supplies evidence that changes the next decision?
terms: A step such as a tool call that affects or queries an environment.

title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
hook: Let a smaller model draft tokens for a larger model to check.
idea: A draft model proposes several tokens; the target model verifies them in parallel with a sampling procedure designed to preserve its output distribution.
analogy: A junior editor drafts a phrase and a senior editor checks the batch, accepting useful work and correcting the rest.
why: It can reduce generation latency without changing the target sampling distribution under the algorithm’s assumptions. Gains depend on acceptance rates and system overhead.
read: Read the algorithm overview and the draft/verify explanation, then inspect speed experiments and assumptions.
question: When does verification cost outweigh the useful draft tokens?
terms: The time a user waits for a response.
The fraction of proposed draft tokens accepted by the verifier.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
hook: Use GPU memory more flexibly when serving many requests.
idea: PagedAttention organizes the key-value cache into blocks that need not occupy contiguous memory. The vLLM system uses this to reduce waste and share cache data when appropriate.
analogy: A library stores a book across available shelves and keeps an index, instead of reserving one oversized continuous shelf for every reader.
why: Better cache management can allow more requests to be processed together. The paper’s throughput gains depend on workload, hardware, baselines and latency constraints.
read: Read the abstract and introduction; study the memory-management figures and system overview. Compare throughput results together with their experimental conditions.
question: Why does serving many different-length conversations waste memory without flexible allocation?
terms: Stored attention information from previous tokens, reused when generating later tokens.
The amount of work completed per unit of time, such as output tokens per second.

title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
hook: Combine compact model storage with small trainable adapters.
idea: QLoRA keeps a frozen base model in 4-bit form and trains low-rank adapters. It adds techniques to reduce memory use during fine-tuning.
analogy: Keep a compact reference edition and learn a small set of corrections instead of storing and rewriting a full-size copy.
why: It lowers memory requirements for adaptation. Compression, training memory and runtime speed are separate concerns, and evaluation results are setup-specific.
read: Read LoRA first. Then study the overview, quantization discussion and memory results; finish with the evaluation caveats.
question: What is compressed, and what is still being learned?
terms: Representing numerical values with fewer bits.
A 4-bit representation designed for normally distributed model weights.

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
hook: Learn directly from preferred and rejected answers.
idea: DPO reformulates a preference-learning objective so that a model can be trained on pairs of preferred and rejected responses without a separately trained reward model and the usual reinforcement-learning loop.
analogy: Show an editor two answers and train toward the preferred one while keeping changes anchored to a reference.
why: It simplifies a route to preference alignment. Results depend on the preference data and objective; preferred does not always mean correct.
read: Read the introduction and method intuition before the derivation, then review the experimental comparisons.
question: What biases could be present in the preference pairs?
terms: Two outputs labeled by which is preferred.
A baseline model used to constrain how far training moves.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
hook: Share key and value information across groups of attention heads.
idea: Grouped-query attention uses fewer key-value heads than query heads. The paper also describes adapting existing multi-head checkpoints through additional training.
analogy: Several readers share one set of reference notes instead of each carrying a complete duplicate.
why: It offers a tradeoff between cache memory, generation speed and model quality. It is an architectural choice, not simply a universal switch for any model.
read: Read the head-grouping diagram and the uptraining recipe, then compare quality and speed together.
question: What do we gain by sharing, and what flexibility might we lose?
terms: One component of a multi-head attention mechanism.
An attention component that produces key and value representations.

title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
hook: Select what to retain in a compact evolving state.
idea: Mamba uses input-dependent state-space updates to selectively retain or forget information, with an algorithm designed for efficient hardware execution.
analogy: Keep updating a working notebook instead of comparing every new sentence against every previous sentence.
why: It explores a different route to sequence modeling with linear sequence-length scaling. Long-context efficiency does not imply equal performance on every task.
read: Read the introduction and selective-state-space intuition, then inspect scaling and language-modeling experiments.
question: What information must a compact state preserve, and what could be lost?
terms: A representation carried forward as a sequence is processed.
Work grows roughly in proportion to sequence length.

title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
hook: Combine sparse experts, compressed attention and training engineering.
idea: The report describes a mixture-of-experts model using Multi-head Latent Attention, low-precision training and other system choices to improve training and inference efficiency.
analogy: A large factory improves its specialist routing, storage and production scheduling together.
why: It is a system-level case study, not evidence that one technique alone explains the result. Reported training figures are not total organizational development costs.
read: Read the introduction, architecture and infrastructure overviews, then separate ablations from whole-system benchmark comparisons.
question: Which efficiency claim comes from architecture, hardware, or training procedure?
terms: Multi-head Latent Attention, which compresses attention-related representations.
Computing with numerical formats that use fewer bits.

title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
hook: Use reinforcement learning and staged training for reasoning tasks.
idea: The report studies R1-Zero with reinforcement learning and R1 with a multi-stage pipeline that includes cold-start data, then distills reasoning behavior into smaller models.
analogy: Practice with checkable outcomes can encourage useful solution strategies; examples can help make the results more readable.
why: It connects reasoning behavior to training incentives and distillation. Benchmark success does not guarantee reliable reasoning on unfamiliar tasks.
read: Compare R1-Zero with R1 before reading the results. Then review distillation experiments and limitations.
question: How do the reward, starting model and training data shape the result?
terms: Training behavior using feedback expressed as rewards.
Training a smaller model using outputs or signals from a larger one.

title: Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup: A New Axis of Sparsity for Large Language Models
hook: Separate some knowledge lookup from neural computation.
idea: Engram adds a conditional memory module with deterministic lookup for recurring local patterns. The paper studies how to divide capacity between this memory and neural computation.
analogy: A specialist keeps frequently used facts in a quick reference drawer instead of deriving each fact again.
why: It explores memory as another axis of sparsity alongside mixture-of-experts computation. Its controlled experiments are research evidence, not proof that lookup replaces reasoning or that every released DeepSeek model uses the same design.
read: Start with the abstract, module diagram and sparsity-allocation experiment. Compare models under the stated parameter and compute constraints.
question: When should a model retrieve a stored pattern, and when should it calculate something new?
terms: A memory component accessed selectively according to the input.
A short sequence of adjacent tokens.

title: Kimi K2.5: Visual Agentic Intelligence
hook: Train text, vision and agent coordination together.
idea: Kimi K2.5 combines text and vision training with an Agent Swarm framework that decomposes some tasks into parallel subtasks.
analogy: A team shares a document and its diagrams, then divides independent research tasks before combining the results.
why: The contribution connects multimodal understanding to agent orchestration. Reported speedups depend on which tasks can be parallelized and on the evaluation setup.
read: Read the model overview and the Agent Swarm section; inspect baselines, resource budgets and where parallelism helps.
question: Which parts of a task are independent enough to run in parallel?
terms: Able to process more than one kind of input, such as text and images.
Multiple coordinated agents working on parts of a larger task.

title: GLM-5: from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering
hook: Improve the training system for longer engineering tasks.
idea: GLM-5 combines sparse attention with asynchronous reinforcement-learning infrastructure and algorithms intended to learn from complex interactions.
analogy: A training workshop lets trainees keep practicing while the teacher updates the lesson plan, instead of making every trainee wait for each update.
why: It connects model efficiency to the infrastructure used for post-training. A stronger agent benchmark score does not by itself establish reliable autonomous engineering.
read: Read the architecture and reinforcement-learning overview, then the long-horizon task evaluations and training-system comparisons.
question: How much of the improvement comes from the model, the training process, or the tools around it?
terms: Reinforcement learning in which experience generation and training need not wait for each other at every step.
Attention that selects part of the available context rather than considering every pair.

title: Attention Residuals
hook: Let layers choose which earlier representations to reuse.
idea: Attention Residuals replaces fixed accumulation of previous layer outputs with learned attention across network depth. A block-based variant reduces memory and communication overhead.
analogy: Instead of adding every colleague’s earlier draft with equal weight, an editor selects the earlier drafts most useful for the current revision.
why: The original Transformer applies attention across sequence positions; this work applies selection across depth. It is a distinct architectural question, not a replacement for every use of token attention.
read: Read the residual-connection motivation, full versus Block AttnRes diagrams, scaling comparisons and ablations.
question: How is choosing earlier layers different from choosing earlier words?
terms: A route that carries an earlier representation forward alongside a layer’s new computation.
The sequence of layers through which a representation passes.

title: Claude Fable 5.2 & Claude Mythos 5.2
hook: How much can a progress indicator change a model’s score?
idea: Anthropic describes Fable and Mythos as two configurations of one model. One experiment lets you isolate the role of the software around Fable. The model took the same programming test twice under different conditions.
analogy: Imagine taking an exam with a countdown clock, then taking it without one. Seeing the time left may change when you finish a draft and hand it in.
why: A benchmark score belongs to a model operating in a particular setup. Reporting what the model could see makes a result easier to interpret and reproduce.
read: Read the first paragraph of PDF page 2 for the relationship between Fable and Mythos. Then go to reader page 216 and compare the two ProgramBench results for Fable 5.2.
question: What would you hold constant to test whether displaying the remaining budget helps your own assistant?
terms: The software that gives a model a task, supplies tools or feedback, and records the result.
A repeatable set of tasks with a defined scoring method.

title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol
hook: What can a collection of reported mistakes tell us?
idea: OpenAI retested earlier conversations in which users had flagged factual problems. One grader checked for any major error in a new response. Another checked whether the specific reported mistake returned.
analogy: If you inspect only the parts that customers returned, you can learn a lot about recurring defects. To estimate the defect rate of all parts shipped, you need a sample from all shipments.
why: How cases enter an evaluation determines which questions its results can answer. The two graders also measure different outcomes in the same answers.
read: Read reader page 72 for the case selection and the graders. On page 73, study the two panels of Figure 25 and the paragraph directly below. The printed page numbers are one lower than the reader counter.
question: Which population would you sample to estimate the frequency of factual errors in everyday use?
terms: Checking a claim against evidence or an explicit acceptance rule.
The comparison system or result against which a new result is judged.

title: Gemini 4 Neon
hook: How much room does a long document leave for an answer?
idea: DeepMind describes Neon as a Gemini 4 Carbon adaptation for recurring work that needs reasoning and efficient execution. The input and generated output draw on one shared context window.
analogy: Think of a single sheet of graph paper. Each row you fill with measurements leaves one fewer row for your calculations.
why: A large advertised context window describes capacity. Planning a document task also requires space for the answer and a check that the answer uses the right evidence.
read: On PDF page 2, read the Inputs and Outputs paragraphs together. Identify the combined window and the default synchronous output limit. Then look for the distinctions between capacity and task performance in Evaluation.
question: How much input could you budget if your answer must have room for 50,000 tokens?
terms: The text or other information available to the model during a request.
A unit used to represent input or output. One token may be a word or part of a word.
